articles.title: Video Game Workers at Blizzard Won First Union Contracts
articles.author: Dan DiMaggio
articles.content: Workers who make some of the world’s most popular video games, including World of Warcraft and Diablo , won their first union contracts in early September, in an important step forward for organizing in the tech industry. The 1,900 workers are employed by Blizzard, which was acquired by Microsoft in 2023 in the largest deal ever in the video game industry. Their new Communications Workers (CWA) contracts include recall rights and guaranteed severance packages for laid-off workers — significant wins, since tech and video game workers have seen waves of layoffs in the last few years. Workers on various Activision Blizzard teams have voted to join CWA since 2022. It started with quality assurance testers at Raven Software — when Raven abruptly laid off a dozen testers in December 2021, they went on strike and launched a union drive. Soon after the Raven workers voted the union in, Microsoft signed a neutrality agreement with CWA, pledging to remain neutral in organizing campaigns and to allow workers and union representatives to communicate openly. In exchange, the union agreed to support the software giant’s purchase of Activision Blizzard, which was facing antitrust scrutiny. Activision Blizzard had also faced employee walkouts and a lawsuit by the California Civil Rights Department in 2021 over claims of misconduct and discrimination against women and a “frat boy” company culture. Next to unionize were quality assurance testers at Blizzard’s offices in Albany, New York, and Austin, Texas. A wall-to-wall unit of five hundred World of Warcraft workers unionized in 2024, followed by units of two hundred game developers at Overwatch , 160 members of Blizzard’s story and franchise team, and 450 Diablo designers, engineers, artists, and support staff in 2025. Recall Rights Blizzard workers won the right to be recalled for fourteen months after being laid off. This right extends to any open positions they are qualified for across the 1,900-worker Blizzard bargaining units. The contracts have separate expiration dates but the same terms across all these units. (The Raven workers, who are part of Activision, already bargained a separate contract.) “We know we are at the start of a labor movement in video games and tech at large,” said Mahreen Fatima, a senior environment artist on Diablo . “So it weighed heavily on us to make sure we set a strong precedent.” CWA has organized four thousand video game workers at Microsoft, and has another 550 members in its industry-wide United Video Game Workers affiliate . The latter is a pre-majority union: it allows video game workers to directly join before winning a union election, a model CWA has employed in organizing public sector and higher education workers in Southern states. Another one hundred game developers behind Magic: The Gathering Arena voted to join CWA in June. In a survey of US video game workers by the Game Developers Conference early this year, 82 percent of respondents supported unionizing. Organizers hope that the protections and job security provisions won at Blizzard will convince more game workers to organize. At Blizzard, laid-off workers will get a minimum of four weeks’ severance plus an additional week for every six months’ tenure, up to thirty-nine weeks. The contract also includes just cause protections, a grievance procedure, and a three-day in-office hybrid workweek. And the union fought hard to put other existing benefits and policies in writing, from weather-related policies to money Blizzard workers are given to spend on the company’s games — all now enforceable through the contract. Blizzard workers also won language that requires the company to discuss, evaluate, and bargain over the impact of artificial intelligence on their work. “Now we have a seat at the table to be part of the conversation when it comes to AI implementation,” said Fatima. “The contract gives us the ability to critically think about how it’s going to impact our workflow, our skill sets, the quality of our product, our teams.” The union won a guarantee that existing remote workers, like Fatima, can continue working remotely, which prevents them from being forced to potentially move across the country to keep their job. Remote workers make up around one-fourth of the workforce covered under the new contract. The contract also includes protections against outsourcing — a Blizzard worker can’t be laid off unless the company has let go any contractor hired in the last year doing a similar job, and a laid-off Blizzard worker can’t be replaced by a contractor for another year. Successorship language in the agreement requires a purchasing company to recognize the union contract if Microsoft decides to sell off the unionized Blizzard units. And in a win that links a new group of workers to one of the labor movement’s oldest traditions, the Blizzard contract includes a paid holiday on May 1, International Workers’ Day. Job Security a Top Issue Job security is a major issue for workers throughout the tech industry. Shortly after Microsoft bought Activision Blizzard for $75 billion in 2023, it announced in January 2024 that it was laying off 1,900 workers in its gaming division — 9 percent of the workforce. This July, Microsoft announced it would be laying off another 3,200 workers in gaming. Half of the layoffs were immediate, including hundreds of CWA members at Bethesda, ZeniMax, and other studios. In August,workers and allies held “Save Our Devs” rallies across the US and Canada to protest the layoffs and demand fair first contracts for Microsoft video game workers. CWA and Microsoft are now bargaining over the effects of these layoffs. The other 1,600 layoffs are expected by the end of 2027. The sense that Blizzard workers were now a part of a bigger company with a more ruthless economic logic was one motivation behind the union effort. “Being in a union stops you from being treated like a line in an Excel sheet,” said Paul Cox, a senior content designer at World of Warcraft who’s been with Blizzard for nineteen years. “We are in a giant corporation, and there is no way that anybody who makes decisions knows everybody in the company.” After years of robust hiring, the entire tech sector has been hit with waves of mass layoffs since 2022. The tracker website layoffs.fyi estimates that tech companies have announced one hundred thousand layoffs in 2026 alone. For years, tech workers were in such demand that employers vied to offer the most appealing benefits and work environment. However, “these days, a position in tech looks like a regular job,” wrote the Wall Street Journal last year. “Workers are contending with the constant fear of layoffs, longer hours, and an ever-growing list of responsibilities for the same pay.” The rapid development of artificial intelligence has only intensified workers’ concerns about being replaced. At Google, 4,700 workers have signed a petition supporting guaranteed severance packages and buyouts before involuntary layoffs. The Alphabet Workers Union, another CWA affiliate, has also organized T-shirt days and mass email actions as part of its “Googlers for Job Security” campaign , launched last year in response to rounds of mass layoffs even as the company remains immensely profitable. The campaign takes credit for Google’s offer of voluntary exit packages to seventy thousand employees — something no other big tech company has done — and is pushing for these buyouts to be offered across the company. Red Shirt Days Blizzard has four US offices, in Austin, Boston, Irvine, and Albany, New York, each with hundreds of workers. The neutrality agreement gave the union access to the facilities. “Because of the neutrality agreement, we were able to set up tables in the courtyard,” said Alison Veneto, a senior editor on the Blizzard story and franchise team who works in the Irvine office. “Everybody moves through there to go from one building to the other, or to go to lunch. So the union was always quite visible.” Blizzard workers embraced the CWA tradition of wearing red on Thursdays, adopted in memory of a striking telephone company worker killed on a picket line in 1989. “The cafeteria would be a sea of red T-shirts,” said Veneto. “You would go into in-person meetings with management and everyone would be wearing their red shirts.” Since these video game workers spend much of their time in front of computer screens, workers showed their support digitally by changing their Zoom backgrounds and Slack profile photos to echo the union’s message. While the workers at Blizzard are on separate teams, they’re all in a large general chat on Slack, a communications platform used to coordinate work within and across teams. There they could post messages of support for the union and the bargaining team en masse. “People would put forward in company chats why unionizing mattered to them,” said Veneto. “That’s why it felt personal — the union doesn’t feel like a third-person entity.” These tactics also helped engage remote workers. “We tried to make as many avenues as possible to include remote workers — we don’t want them to feel excluded,” said Fatima, who works remotely from Seattle. The organizing committee arranged union info sessions for remote workers, and put Outlook invites onto everyone’s work calendar so they couldn’t miss it. Pattern Bargaining At first the different Blizzard bargaining units were negotiating separately with Microsoft, although the bargaining committees were in communication with each other. As they pushed for first contracts, workers organized numerous marches across Blizzard’s Irvine campus with members from all the bargaining units. They held sign-making parties in view of executive offices, and a sit-in on the executive floor. But gradually, workers recognized that the World of Warcraft unit, the largest, would set the standard — so the union started to focus its mobilization efforts there. In the end, Microsoft agreed to a union proposal to extend the terms it had agreed to with the World of Warcraft unit to other Blizzard workers. One factor that likely weighed on management was the possibility of disruptive action at BlizzCon — the annual convention to promote Blizzard’s games, which draws forty thousand attendees to the Anaheim Convention Center. This year’s convention was held September 11–13, just days after the union agreement was reached.

articles.title: According to Polls, Americans Like Socialism a Lot
articles.author: Branko Marcetic
articles.content: Socialism is more popular than it’s been for a long time, both socialism and its most well-known adherents appeal to a surprisingly diverse voter base, and most people still have no idea who Hasan Piker is. Those are just a few of the takeaways from a crop of polls conducted over the past month or so, which together suggest the radicalized, antiestablishment zeal that’s taken over the Democratic electorate and opened the door for a rising socialist insurgency is still going strong, with a few surprises in tow. And they come at a potentially crucial time, as socialist Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez weighs whether to make a run for president in 2028, a campaign that many socialists view as pivotal to the future prospects of their movement as a whole. We should obviously be careful with polls, which are not actual elections and only give us an imperfect snapshot of public opinion at any point in time. Still, while they may not exactly reflect hard numbers, they do often reflect real trends, especially when put alongside other poll results. And as such, these recent ones offer several takeaways. Socialism Is Surprisingly Popular . . . A new Gallup poll conducted over the month of August puts socialism at its highest positive rating, 43 percent, since the polling firm started asking Americans in 2010. Socialism has hovered just under the 40 point mark every year since, until experiencing a pronounced uptick since last year. Maybe more significant is the reason for this uptick, which according to Gallup isn’t to do with the attitudes of Democrats — their roughly two-thirds positive view has effectively stayed flat since last year — but thanks to independents , whose positive views of socialism have gone 8 points up to 45 percent. To be clear, socialism still has a way to go. The same Gallup poll found that capitalism is viewed significantly more positively at 55 percent, effectively unchanged from last year, as is “free enterprise” at 77 percent — which, somewhat confusingly, fell 4 points since last year, part of a more gradual downward slide it’s experienced since 2019. On the other hand, “big business” is in the doldrums, hitting a new low of 35 percent this year. And socialism’s appeal remains geographically specific. According to a recent New York Times /Siena University poll of likely voters nationwide, socialism’s favorability is underwater in all four regions polled but is strongest in the West (-8), and weakest in the South (-27). In a Times /Siena poll of Michigan specifically later this month, Detroit was the only region where it was close to breaking even (-1). Nevertheless, though 43 percent isn’t a majority, recent history shows that may not matter. Less than a quarter (24 percent) of Americans viewed the MAGA movement positively in April 2023, a year and a half before Donald Trump and MAGA routed the Democrats and took total control of the federal government. The Gallup results here track with several other recent polls that show voters are significantly more open to voting for a socialist candidate than a MAGA politician. . . . and Popular With a Surprising Coalition The general narrative is that socialism is mostly popular with young, well-off, and highly educated white progressives. This recent wave of survey results does continue to show there’s a marked generational divide in socialist support. But other than that, this narrative about socialism being confined to a particular demographic slice isn’t really supported by the data. In the Gallup poll, socialism has more support from people of color and those earning less than $100,000 than from white adults and those earning more than that figure. And its support is about the same whether someone went to college or not. In fact, other than adults aged thirty-four and younger, people of color are the only group that views socialism more positively than capitalism. We saw a similar result in the Times /Siena nationwide poll, in which white voters had the least favorable view of socialism (-26), followed by the “other non-white” category (-18), while black and Latino voters viewed it most favorably (+4 for each). Interestingly, that poll does show an educational divide, but one that breaks down along race: while white voters of any educational level hold a very dim view of socialism (a net negative in the double digits), non-white voters both with college degrees (-4) and without (0) hold much more positive views. Bear in mind that only 18 percent of the voters surveyed in that poll self-identified as democratic socialists, with the highest proportion of those that did (33 percent) being non-white, non-college-educated voters. AOC and Zohran Have Different Coalitions The data is particularly interesting when we move away from socialism writ large and look at specific social ists , especially two of the most high-profile socialist politicians: possible 2028 presidential contender Rep. Ocasio-Cortez and New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani. Both are wildly popular with what have come to be termed “normie” Democrats. The Liberal Currents survey found that the pair, as well as fellow socialist Sen. Bernie Sanders, officially an independent, are three of the most popular figures in the Democratic Party, behind names like Barack Obama, Kamala Harris, Pete Buttigieg, and Gavin Newsom. Meanwhile, the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), the organization that counts both Ocasio-Cortez and Mamdani as members and that has been involved in many of the left-insurgent victories this past year — holds a net +53 positive rating, with its strongest favorability (+45) coming from black voters. But when it comes to views of Ocasio-Cortez and Mamdani, there seems to be a divide between Democratic and all other voters. Comparing the Liberal Currents and Times /Siena poll, we can summarize some of the takeaways as follows: Ocasio-Cortez is viewed slightly more favorably than Mamdani by Democratic voters, while Mamdani is viewed substantially more favorably than Ocasio-Cortez by all likely voters (Ocasio-Cortez has an overall -11 rating from the latter). In both cases, Ocasio-Cortez substantially lags Mamdani in terms of her support from younger voters, meaning those aged under forty-five. Mamdani has a stronger favorability with independents and nonvoters (+14 with each), raising the question of whether the New York mayor’s rise helps explain independents’ growing friendliness to socialism since last year. As with socialism more generally, when it comes to all likely voters, both get their strongest support from voters of color and especially black voters, college-educated and not. Ocasio-Cortez is significantly stronger with Latino voters, while Mamdani is stronger with the “other, non-white” category, maybe related to his campaign’s unprecedented mobilization of South Asian voters. These demographic coalitions look very different when it comes to just Democratic voters: there Ocasio-Cortez has her highest favorability with white voters and also beats Mamdani with black voters, but significantly lags him among Latino voters. (By contrast, Sanders registers a stronger rating than the pair among all three voter groups.) Put aside these details, and the broader takeaway is that the country’s most well-known socialists derive their strongest support from non-white voters and have significant appeal to those among them without a college education. By contrast, DSA, the nation’s largest socialist organization, is according to its most recent internal polling 60 percent white — down from 85 percent five years ago — as well as 9 percent black and 14 percent Latino. In older surveys , a substantial share of its members had or worked in fields that required higher education degrees, though like the racial demographics, that has likely changed in the years since. Still, these poll results suggest the organization’s struggle to diversify its membership is not due to some inherent aversion to socialism by non-white and non-college-educated Americans. It suggests these efforts may bear further fruit — but that it may also require changes within its own recruitment practices and internal culture. The Democratic Party Has Been Ideologically Transformed We are a long way away from the pre-2016 era, when Democrats largely didn’t think about politics in ideological terms. These poll results show that not only have Sanders’s two presidential runs and the Democratic establishment’s series of failures transformed and radicalized the Democratic electorate, but that they’ve done so in a way that leaves a socialist candidate with the strongest pitch to make them. The Liberal Currents survey confirms what countless polls have told us over the past nearly two years, namely that Democratic voters have had it with their own leadership. Senate leader Chuck Schumer has only a +3 net positive rating from Democrats, while possible future House Speaker Hakeem Jeffries is disliked by 22 percent of them. These voters agree with the statement that “criticizing the Democratic Party establishment makes you more likely to support a candidate” by a +19 margin. On a policy level, the survey shows Democratic voters are strongly in favor of positions that socialist politicians have long taken: expanding the Supreme Court, abolishing the filibuster, zoning reform to build more housing (an issue socialists have long led on ), holding the line on trans rights, and taxing billionaires out of existence, with Democratic voters believing billionaires shouldn’t exist by a 6 point margin. Note that not all of this newly radicalized electorate’s views necessarily line up with what might be socialist priorities: these voters are overwhelmingly friendly toward the idea of a military coup against Trump and double the share of self-described liberal voters want Trump officials prosecuted by the next administration as socialist or progressive ones do. In any case, whether or not she decides to run, Ocasio-Cortez is the socialist politician best positioned to capitalize on this transformation and not just because numerous polls show she’s now one of the party’s leading figures. Not only does the Liberal Currents survey show she has strong support from young voters when matched up head-to-head with the rest of the potential field, but crucially, she retains high favorables (+52) with voters over forty-five and white voters (+54) — a demographic that votes heavily in primaries, and whose skepticism of Sanders sunk both of his presidential campaigns. The next most progressive likely 2028 contender, California Democrat Ro Khanna, lags behind her with all these demographics and has far lower name recognition. To deflect against the inevitable electability arguments, Ocasio-Cortez will be able to point out that her positions are broadly popular with the electorate. Voters nationwide, in Michigan , and in other battleground states all prefer candidates who oppose military aid to Israel. In Michigan, voters prefer a pro–Medicare for All candidate by 29 points. These voters also hate data centers and want them limited and heavily regulated. Other polls show even self-described moderate voters holding stridently anti-billionaire views, and swing voters being more likely to back a candidate who wants to tax the rich, pass Medicare for All, and raise the minimum wage. Especially significant is that more than 81 percent of Democratic voters believe a candidate’s foreign policy views are important. This doesn’t just mean the matter of Israel-Palestine, which socialists have led on. The same poll found these voters oppose a US war with China over Taiwan by a 16 point margin, part of a wider trend in US public opinion that views China less negatively and is less predisposed to conflict with the country. “The Discourse” Is Not (Always) Real Life Finally, there’s long been a lot of talk about how the pet obsessions of the press and social media commentators don’t really reflect what most average people are thinking about. This has always veered into overstatement — there is every sign that people are thinking and worrying about artificial intelligence to a similar degree as pundits and online chatterers, for instance. But it is definitely true when it comes to some of the leading controversies of this election season. Take Twitch streamer Hasan Piker, who, despite holding no elected office or any formal power at all, has become a media fixation. One aggregator found that news outlets had published 327 stories about Piker over the last three months, or more than three stories per day, the vast majority of it in national coverage. Yet polls show most voters still have no idea who he is. Fifty-one percent of Democratic voters have never heard of him, even though centrist Democrats have worked to put him at the center of both primary and now general election contests. More astoundingly, 54 percent of specifically Michigan voters haven’t heard of him, even though you would assume from media coverage he’s the most important issue in that race. For that matter, 69 percent of Democratic voters have never heard of DSA national Cochair Megan Romer, whose recent interview missteps were a big story among the commentariat last month but don’t appear to have resonated elsewhere. It’s hard to know exactly what to make of this, but one explanation could be that it signals the waning power of traditional news. Cable news networks saw their ratings nosedive last year, and things haven’t been much better a year later, part of a longer-term decline that ticked up after Trump’s 2025 win. It goes beyond viewership: trust in traditional forms of media fell last year to an all-time low . Given the role corporate and legacy news outlets have played in tilting previous election results, including presidential ones, this could prove advantageous for left insurgents and other outsider candidates. An Altered Landscape So, to recap: socialism and socialists are slowly but surely growing in mainstream approval, that approval is often strongest among people of color and isn’t limited to college graduates, and the Democratic and general voter electorate have been transformed in ways that have flung the doors open to socialist ideas and organizing wider than they’ve been in a very long time. Oh, and constantly bringing up Hasan Piker does not seem to be the political silver bullet that Republicans and corporate Democrats want it to be. There’s a long way to go before 2028, and all of this could look different in the wake of whatever happens in November, not to mention after whatever potential wild card a Trump who no longer cares about elections ends up playing. Still, it’s clear the past ten years of socialist organizing have slowly, unevenly reshaped the US political landscape — and that landscape in turn is changing the fortunes for socialist organizing.

articles.title: Literacy Is Another Casualty of the Decline of Democracy
articles.author: John Livesey
articles.content: Approximately two years ago, a bizarre new genre of AI-generated content began to emerge online. Suddenly social media was filled with short-form videos depicting hypersexual anthropomorphic fruit, embroiled in increasingly far-fetched and soapy plot lines. In one video, a voluptuous strawberry cheats on her watermelon husband, and gives birth to two wolf cubs. In another, an emasculated orange takes revenge on a womanizing banana who has stolen his girlfriend. In a particularly violent iteration, a young tangerine is bullied by his homophobic father and ends up juicing his whole family. It is easy to dismiss these shlocky and incoherent narratives as mere “AI slop.” But they are also endemic to a broader culture. In 2026, the average American spends at least two hours a day doomscrolling — significantly more time than Asians and Europeans, whose social media use is in decline. On their phones, shirtless celebrities, videos of bears chasing cyclists, or children buried under the rubble of their family home are all part of an undifferentiated stream. Faced with this endless churn of content, the human attention span has become increasingly fragmented. Our ability to register nuance and complexity has also taken a hit. So it is that millions find themselves engaging with mindless dross from Baby Shark for toddlers to Fruit Love Island for adults. What, one might ask, is the cost of this new form of consumption? The answer, argues British journalist James Marriott in The New Dark Ages , is human literacy. Marriott describes his book as an “impassioned attack on the trivial and meaningless culture of the screen and a defence of the written word.” There can be no doubt that Marriott has picked a hot-button topic. Evidence of declining literacy rates is stark. In 2004, almost 30 percent of Americans read for pleasure; by 2023, that figure had fallen to just 16 percent. Books are getting shorter, comprehension of long words is in decline, and many young people now source their politics from TikTok, YouTube, and Instagram. Of course, warnings about mass media consumption are nothing new; experts have been issuing warnings since the dawn of television in the 1950s. To his credit, Marriott attempts to look beyond headline figures by situating the current crisis of literacy within a broader history and asking whether the rejection of printed media is a form of cultural evolution — a turn to what some have called “secondary literacy” — or a more concerning indication of civilizational decline. Too often, however, The New Dark Ages shies away from big ideas; Marriott himself seems more comfortable reproducing aggregate statistics than offering granular analysis. The result is a frustrating and often shortsighted work: a defense of elite culture that has very little to say about the economic or political forces that have produced the current crisis in literacy or those that might help to resolve it. The Democratization of Literacy The New Dark Ages starts by taking us back more than three thousand years to the first recorded instances of written language in ancient Mesopotamia. “Reading was by no means inevitable,” he observes. This is something of an understatement. Even today there remains no evidence to suggest that humans were ever cognitively programmed to understand the patterns of signs and symbols that we have come to call language. To develop these advanced linguistic abilities, we had to retrain our brains: an immensely difficult and time-consuming process that ensured that reading and writing remained the preserve of a specialized elite for over three millennia. There is evidence to suggest that literacy rates increased during the more prosperous centuries of the Roman Empire. By some measures, approximately 10 to 15 percent of the population could read. However, these numbers would stagnate for much of the Middle Ages. In Europe, it was not until the invention of the modern movable-type printing press by Johannes Gutenberg in 1440 that mass literacy was even remotely conceivable, although even then its growth was gradual. In the words of the sixteenth-century essayist Francis Bacon, Gutenberg’s invention (alongside gunpowder and the compass) had “changed the appearance and state of the world” by disseminating print culture throughout Europe. No doubt this process was helped by the spread of Lutheran Protestant ideas that offered a cultural argument for literacy as a tool of social emancipation. So began an era of mass “democratization.” Marriott — a self-described “Enlightenment bro” — pays particularly close attention to the eighteenth century, an era in which the growth of literacy helped many to challenge existing forms of religious and political authority, remaking the world according to new modes of rationalism. Books, journals, newspapers, and pamphlets spread information that might previously have been accessible only by the elite but that could now be turned against them. Marriott has little patience for the strand of Enlightenment skepticism one finds among the likes of Theodor Adorno and Max Horkheimer. For those thinkers, the rationalistic quantification and measurement of social reality allowed humans to dominate one another in ways previously unimaginable. Marriott contents himself with cheering Voltaire — a man who “dared to know” — and the democratic energy, as opposed to economic and social forces, that led to the first French Revolution. The cult of the written word continued to grow until the middle of the twentieth century, when television challenged the novel’s place as the main means of imagining a shared cultural community. In 1985, Neil Postman’s Amusing Ourselves to Death sought to explain this drastic cultural shift. For him, TV’s tendency toward triviality, spectacle, and celebrity had hijacked the attention of its consumers and eroded the calmer and more rational forms of thought that reading promoted. Postman was particularly dismissive of the phrase “Now. . . . this,” which in TV-speak tied one form of entertainment to another. This uniquely modern idiom, he remarked, served to highlight how disjointed and banal TV programming had become; the new medium encouraged viewers to passively absorb the diffuse fragments of information that were being beamed into their households. Postman’s analysis of the “Now. . . . this” paradigm seems particularly relevant today. If TV crowded out the time needed to pick up a book, the invention of the desktop computer and, later, the smartphone has dealt a near-fatal blow to the culture of reading. Suddenly the options for entertainment are infinite, and all accessible literally at our fingertips. On TikTok, users are able to skip through 260 videos in under thirty-five minutes. Meanwhile the latest developments in phone software encourage “dual screening” or “in-picture watching” — marketing jargon for being able to text, call, or browse while watching films on devices. Producers at Netflix have even encouraged their filmmakers to insert plot refreshers into dialogue throughout any production, better for those not paying attention to catch up easily. A Cultural Crisis? The New Dark Ages is at its best when describing the dangerous effects that these new behaviors might have on our ability to think critically. When we read, Marriott observes, we can engage in a number of sophisticated cognitive processes: drawing inferences, assessing truth value, considering multiple perspectives, and integrating everything into a broader analysis that allows us to interpret meaning and make judgements of aesthetic quality. Unlike short-form videos, books exercise the human attention span. They challenge us to follow a line of thought to its logical conclusions, for instance. This makes writing a particularly subtle form of expression, capable of holding nuance and contradiction unlike more visual media. As greater numbers of people turn to digital entertainment, however, these cognitive skills are under threat. Consider again the phenomenon of AI fruit videos. They pander to the shallowest human desires: providing an emotionally saturated spectacle, complete with bright colors, unexpected narrative twists, and thinly veiled forms of sexual taboo. A similar degeneration is evident in our politics. Data shows that political speeches given in parliaments across the West are getting shorter. However, they are also getting louder, using quasi-hysterical appeals to a public that is no longer able to process or participate in any other form of rational debate. As Marriott rightly observes, this highly affective politics is embodied by President Donald Trump who, by no coincidence, refuses to read memos or policy briefs on principle. It is hard to disagree with Marriott, even if he at points seems to offer an unintended example of the declining literary culture he is mourning. His sentences are often clipped and written in simple journalistic prose, appropriate for a seven-hundred-word column but not a serious study of the decline in literacy. The New Dark Age is brisk, concise, and peppered with personal anecdotes — perfectly suited to our almost postliterate era. There is also a talking-you-off-the-cliff-edge reasonableness that pervades The New Dark Age . Constantly, we are told that its author has no desire to be “apocalyptic” or “virtuous”; every description of structural crises is followed by evenhanded qualification. “This is not to say” is a common refrain. The this-but-also-that quality of The New Dark Age is attributable to the author’s political outlook. Marriott is a journalist at the right-wing Times newspaper, incapable of thinking seriously about class. One searches the book in vain for any discussion of the relationship between inequality and the crisis of literacy. Studies conducted by Ofcom, a UK media regulator, have shown that low-income families watch twice as much TV and spend significantly longer on social media each day than their wealthier counterparts. Why is this? As many parents have pointed out in response to social media bans in both the UK and Australia, screen time is a begrudged substitute for twenty-four-hour childcare. The growth of the screen-free childhood movement, adopted disproportionately by wealthier parents, has only worsened the disparities between children from different class backgrounds. Childhood is increasingly two-tiered. Some kids spend hours on social media every day, while others have parents who are happy to read them the classics, in some cases even while they are still in the womb. Unsurprisingly, Marriott pulls his punches when it comes to apportioning responsibility for the current crisis in literacy. It is now widely understood that capturing users’ attention — and refusing to let go — is part of the business model of tech billionaires. The longer we spend looking at our phones, the more ads we are exposed to and the more metadata we hand over to internet companies. This means that there is a clear financial incentive to use the algorithm to keep us looking, liking, tapping, and scrolling. As the Google whistleblower Tristan Harris has ominously observed, “you can try having self-control, but there are a thousand engineers on the other side of the screen working against you.” Declining rates of literacy ultimately help Big Tech companies to continue exploiting their consumers without requiring their consent. Instead of identifying and criticizing these trends, Marriott is keener to extol the virtues of Western literature. “We face the serious possibility that writers like Shakespeare, John Milton, and Jane Austen. . . . are not going to reach the next generation of readers,” he writes with glib sanctimony. This seems unlikely. The elite culture that Marriott feels so protective of is not going anywhere; we will always live in a world in which there are places to read the classics — at least for some. What is at stake is the existence of the mass culture, a unique historical development that came into existence only within the last hundred years, when working class people, women, and non-Westerners shaped global politics collectively for the first time. From the Nobel Prize–winning poetry of Rabindranath Tagore to the revolutions that humiliated European imperialism in nations as distinct as Algeria and China, the culture to which mass literacy gave rise was always a by-product of the struggle for, and achievements of, mass democracy. It was and remains the only successful challenge to Western chauvinism and the navel-gazing court culture that has flourished everywhere in the absence of inspiration from the popular classes. Without a renewal of the fight for democracy, we are unlikely to see a return to the culture of informed engagement with the world. If this happens, the end of literacy may be the least of our worries.

articles.title: The San Jose Execution
articles.author: Silicon Valley DSA
articles.content: This statement was written by members of the Silicon Valley DSA Liberation and Justice Working Group . A Tragedy of Systemic Violence The events that unfolded on January 21st, 2026, in San Jose, California, serve as a chilling, visceral testament to the enduring crisis of systemic violence against Black lives in America. Mohamed Husein was a son, a brother, and a father murdered in cold blood for fleeing from San Jose Police Department officers to avoid arrest for a crime spree. He was literally running for his life, attempting to escape a system that, for far too many, equates criminality with a death sentence. The Lethal Pursuit While running away, Mohamed Husein was struck by gunshots that erupted from multiple officers. These bullets found their mark, and Mohamed collapsed onto the street. What happened next was incomprehensible brutality that led to San Jose Police Department SUV, purportedly an instrument of public safety, barreled over his prone body, treating a human life as nothing more than an unseen speed bump. The scene did not end there as it devolved into a firing squad. Gunfire filled the air as the officers discharged their weapons into Mohamed’s already lifeless body that lay in the street. Other than involuntary final jerks of his limbs, the bullets still traveled through his motionless body. This incident is a prime example of a public execution that is a systemic pattern of violence against Black and Brown communities nationwide. State Sanctioned Lynchings: A Grim American Tradition The ruthless slaying of Black people in public view is a grim tradition as old as the United States itself. Historically, the suffering and exploitation of Black and Brown people laid the foundation for America, a parasitic relationship that continues to stunt the growth and potential of these communities. These continued acts of violence against Black and Brown folk must be recognized for what they are: lynchings. Calling them anything else is doing a disservice to those who have fallen at the hands of this broken system, and minimizes the true extent of harm caused to these communities. These highly visible public lynchings have become so common that American society has grown desensitized to the spectacle of Black and Brown lives being extinguished in plain sight. This normalization of violence mirrors the acceptance of historical lynchings in earlier eras, where the public display of Black death served as a tool of terror, social control, and grotesque entertainment. Historically, lynchings served as social control, a threat to all Brown and Black folks who dared to defy the system. The ruling class knew that, without socially normalized lynching, their continued exploitation of Brown and Brown bodies would come to an end. Likewise, we today are inundated with reports of fatal encounters with the police, placing all blame on the victims. Society has become numb to this senseless violence and has begun to accept it as something that “just happens”. Modern-day Lynchings in the Courtroom and the Street Modern-day lynchings have occurred covertly within courtrooms across the nation, carried out under the pretexts of “law and order” and “crime and punishment.” These lynchings have inured the public to the violence the police inflict. Members of the justice system have long used this regime of criminalization as an excuse to manipulate, amend, and blatantly violate the very laws they swore to uphold. Society has widely accepted that law enforcement can, and will, operate outside the boundaries of the law they ostensibly uphold. History is full of examples where minor infractions have been systematically and lethally escalated into death sentences. In the pre-Civil Rights Jim Crow era, social rules demanded subservience from Black folks, like stepping off sidewalks for white people, avoiding eye contact, or speaking informally. The punishment for violations was often brutal lynching rather than due process. The horrific 1943 murder of 15-year-old Willie James Howard in Florida, killed for the “crime” of giving a white girl an innocent Christmas card, illustrates how minor interactions were seen as deadly threats against the structure of white supremacy. Despite being officially abolished, the spirit and consequence of these Jim Crow laws persist today. Recent victims include Eric Garner, Sandra Bland, and George Floyd, who were murdered by the police for such minor alleged crimes as selling loose cigarettes, forgetting to use a turn signal, or using a fake $20 bill. Tragically, this list of victims continues to grow. “Breaking the Law” as a Death Penalty Pretext Today, “breaking the law” may as well lead to the death penalty. By claiming a law has been broken, law enforcement justify circumventing constitutionally guaranteed due process, allowing officers to act as judge, jury, and executioner in the streets. Mohamed Husein was murdered because he was Black, and because the system has made it acceptable to extinguish Black lives, especially when they are alleged to have broken the law. In this country, Black folks are a target of systemic aggression, which is only amplified by a criminal allegation. Once law enforcement labels a victim a criminal, a deeply ingrained societal justification, “if they would not have committed the crime, they would not have been killed”, tacitly sanctions state-sponsored murder. Demanding Accountability in Santa Clara County This county, like others throughout the country, has historically been complacent during public lynchings and has shown a profound lack of regard for the victims of police violence. Excessive force is normalized, especially once a crime is attached to the life taken. In these cases, the Constitutional right of “innocent until proven guilty” becomes a hollow phrase. Jeff Rosen, District Attorney in Santa Clara County, meant to be the community’s advocate for accountability, clearly has misplaced priorities. Instead of pursuing justice for Mohamed, his office sought the only felony charges against pro-Palestine college campus protests in the nation, targeting the Stanford 11;outrageously, he attempted to charge a student reporter, a clear first amendment violation. Rosen was so clearly compromised that his office was barred from re-trying the case since he used it as fundraising for his campaign and tried to paint the protestors as anti-semitic. Months later, there has not been any resolution or justice for the killing of Mohamed, as any elected DA should have achieved by now. The force used in SJPD’s public execution of Mohamed Husein was undeniably excessive. District Attorney Jeff Rosen and his investigative team must bring criminal charges against all deputies involved: the officers shot into his back as he was running, the deputy who ran him over with the SUV, and all the officers who fired into his lifeless body afterwards. They must be prosecuted for taking the law into their own hands instead of following due process and for attempting to rationalize their racist, discriminatory, abhorrent behavior. The Violation of Oath and Law The San Jose Police Department failed to uphold their oath to protect and serve. They ignored their training and did not properly follow the escalation of force process. SJPD possesses several K9 units, which are specifically equipped and trained to apprehend someone fleeing a crime scene without resorting to lethal force, which they could have used to avoid needless death. The punishment of death was not commensurate with the crime committed and would not have been the sentence in any court in California. SJPD broke the law when they executed Mohamed in the street, despite the death penalty moratorium imposed by Governor Gavin Newsom in 2019. Mohamed Husein was denied the dignity of a fair legal process and his constitutionally guaranteed day in court. Instead, he was subjected to the death penalty, a punishment not administered in California, carried out by the very agents sworn to protect him. Addressing the Mental Health Crisis At the root of many instances of brutality by SJPD (and the justice system at large) is society’s failure to adequately support folks experiencing mental health crises, like Mohamed Husein, and many others suffering under this system. Mohahmed’s family informed the police that he was mentally unstable and would require additional assistance or, at least, a modicum of understanding, but even those preemptive warnings were not enough to guarantee safe, non-lethal interactions with law enforcement. Husein’s story, along with those of many others before him, have fomented a deep mistrust in the justice system. Despite that, there seems to be little support for its victims. Many can afford neither the time nor the resources to seek help. Law enforcement often becomes involved when mental illness pushes people past their breaking point. Police are often the first public resource utilized during a crisis. The SJPD has Mobile Crisis Response teams that can respond to mental health crises, but those teams lack crucial resources. Most officers are not adequately trained or equipped to deal with a mental health crisis in a safe manner. We must direct vital funding towards community care programs like the Mobile Crisis Response teams. There are resources available for those seeking help, although visibility and funding for their work is often less than ideal. Within Santa Clara County, there are several organizations that offer accessible mental health support. 988 is the Santa Clara County Crisis and Suicide Hotline , available 24 hours, 7 days a week. Asian Americans for Community Involvement (AACI) is another organization that provides low-to-no cost service available for those seeking help. Trust Mental Health is another organization that offers low-to-no cost services. If you want to organize for a better world, join the Liberation and Justice Working Group of Silicon Valley DSA . articles.title: Greece’s Neo-Nazis Are Back
articles.author: Georgios Samaras
articles.content: For over seven years after it entered parliament in May 2012, Golden Dawn was at the heart of Greece’s political life. Its rise was accompanied by scenes that should have made its character unmistakable. During the June 2012 election campaign, MP Ilias Kasidiaris assaulted two female left-wing politicians live on TV, while numerous other key members were documented openly expressing admiration for Adolf Hitler . Beyond parliament, something far darker was taking place. Golden Dawn was not simply an extremist political party but, a Greek court would later establish, a criminal organization orchestrating a web of violence. Its notorious assault squads terrorized migrants and political opponents across Athens, and its members were implicated in some of the most infamous killings of the period, including the murders of antifascist rapper Pavlos Fyssas and Pakistani migrant worker Shahzad Luqman . The judicial crackdown that followed in September 2013 led to one of the most consequential political trials in modern Greek history. Beginning in April 2015, the proceedings dragged on for more than five years before, in October 2020, Golden Dawn was found to have operated as a criminal organization . Most of its senior leadership received prison sentences of around thirteen years. Kasidiaris is returning to a very different Greece from the one in which Golden Dawn first surged in 2012. Some of the ideas that once marked his party as an extremist outlier have since entered the political mainstream. Golden Dawn may not have an active political presence anymore, but the soil that allowed it to take root is still there. The Trial and Its Aftermath Golden Dawn always cast its leaders as political prisoners, and portrayed the trial as a politically motivated witch hunt . Nikos Michaloliakos, Golden Dawn’s founder, was allowed to leave prison for house arrest on health grounds in September last year, less than five years after his jailing following the verdict. Last Tuesday, Kasidiaris walked free too, less than six years after receiving a thirteen-and-a-half-year sentence for directing a criminal organization. In the past six years, Kasidiaris has been very busy . After his own party “Hellenes” was barred from the 2023 election, he backed the previously unknown Spartans, propelling them instantly into parliament with just one viral tweet . In 2025, Greece’s Special Highest Court ruled that he had effectively acted as the party’s concealed leader . But when he was considered for release, this political activity apparently did not count as a disciplinary violation, raising serious questions about how such conduct was treated by judicial authorities. The differences between Golden Dawn and Kasidiaris’s later political vehicles are deliberate. He has largely abandoned overt Nazi symbolism, despite his documented neo-Nazi past and swastika tattoo, instead repackaging his politics in the language of ultranationalism. Hellenes, for example, called themselves defenders of Greek national sovereignty, while the Spartans avoided explicit identification with Golden Dawn — although several of their 2023 candidates and MPs had previous ties to that party. Last Tuesday, Kasidiaris walked out of Domokos Prison to cheers from dozens of male supporters, posing for photographs and selfies before announcing his return to the “front line” of Greek politics. Wearing a black Fred Perry shirt — a brand whose black-and-yellow polo was notoriously appropriated by the Proud Boys — he promised the emergence of a new “powerful national party.” That return may already command considerably more support than the published polling suggests. I have confidentially reviewed the raw datasets of two separate polls privately conducted by major Greek polling companies over the past month, both of which tested support for a hypothetical Kasidiaris-linked party. One poll put the figure at around 6 percent, the other at 8 percent. Neither appeared in the companies’ published results, however, with both effectively buried within vaguely defined “other” categories. However, a smaller polling firm released its findings on September 21, suggesting that Kasidiaris could secure up to 17 percent of the vote. Withholding figures of that magnitude from public-facing polling risks obscuring politically important information. A convicted neo-Nazi is returning from prison with an electoral constituency potentially large enough to reshape Greek far-right politics and revive a movement many believed had been defeated. Fertile Ground Thirteen years ago, as Golden Dawn was establishing its position during the height of the crisis period, sections of the Greek commentariat openly wondered whether the country needed a “more serious” version of the neo-Nazi party. In September 2013, journalist Babis Papadimitriou — who would later become a New Democracy MP — publicly asked why a “ more serious Golden Dawn” could not support a conservative governing coalition. In many ways, that wish has since been realized. Successive governments under Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis and his right-wing New Democracy have elevated politicians who passed through the far-right ultraorthodox LAOS party into some of the most powerful positions in the state. Adonis Georgiadis, once a LAOS MP, is today both health minister and a vice president of New Democracy. Thanos Plevris, another former LAOS politician, has been Greece’s minister for migration and asylum since 2025. Plevris is also the son of Konstantinos Plevris, one of the most notorious figures of Greece’s postwar far right, a Holocaust denier who has openly described himself as a Nazi and fascist. Thanos’s own record on migration is grim. In 2011, he argued that border protection could not exist without deaths . In the same speech, he advocated denying undocumented migrants food, water, health care, and social assistance, with the explicit aim of making life in Greece so unbearable that it would deter others from coming. Plevris also announced a doctrine of “ prison or return ” for people without a right to remain and described arrivals from North Africa as an “invasion.” These are precisely the kinds of ideas that once distinguished Golden Dawn from Greece’s conventional right. Golden Dawn’s migration politics rested on deterrence through dehumanization of migrants as an existential threat to the nation. What was politically radioactive in 2012 can now be spoken from inside a government ministry almost without consequence, a sign of how much of Golden Dawn’s political language has seeped into the state itself. Seen against the broader European mainstreaming of the far right, Greece is far from the exception it is sometimes portrayed as being by media outlets broadly sympathetic to the government. Golden Dawn disappeared, but the far-right political space became very populated. Greek Solution and the ultraconservative Niki are still represented in the Greek Parliament and Voice of Reason in the European Parliament. MPs elected for Spartans are still sitting as independents after the party’s group collapsed following the ruling by the Special Highest Court. The far-right field may soon become more crowded still. Right-wing former Prime Minister Antonis Samaras has spent much of this year teasing the prospect of yet another party, recasting himself as the aggrieved guardian of the nation. His speeches increasingly revolve around denunciations of the “woke agenda,” delivered with the theatrical indignation of a politician apparently determined to present yesterday’s culture-war slogans as an urgent national emergency. A Trojan Horse In August, Kasidiaris’s brother Alexandros, himself a former Golden Dawn member, filed a declaration with Greece’s Supreme Court establishing a new party. It was formally unveiled on September 21 as the Alliance of Greeks. Little is known so far beyond the identities of a handful of leadership figures and prospective candidates, while Ilias Kasidiaris has yet to clarify what role, if any, he will play. Under the electoral framework introduced in 2023, constitutional experts argue that he cannot formally lead a party until 2033. Nor is simply installing somebody else as leader necessarily enough, as the Supreme Court can examine a party’s real leadership and disqualify it if Kasidiaris is found to be directing it from behind the scenes. But perhaps much of the damage has already been done. Kasidiaris has repeatedly demonstrated how insufficient these restrictions can be. Could a convicted neo-Nazi continue conducting politics from prison? He did. Could his statements circulate through social media while he remained incarcerated? They did. Could he boost another party into parliament while formally remaining outside its leadership? The Spartans provided that experiment. Even Elon Musk entered the story in July, publicly criticizing Kasidiaris’s continued imprisonment. In 2023, writing in the Greek left-wing newspaper Efimerida ton Syntakton , I argued that the Greek state was living under the illusion that legal restrictions alone could prevent Golden Dawn’s political return. One of the main government figures defending the 2023 legislation designed to block Kasidiaris was Makis Voridis, then interior minister. Decades earlier, Voridis had led the youth wing of EPEN , the far-right party founded from prison by former dictator Georgios Papadopoulos — taking over a position previously held by Golden Dawn founder Nikos Michaloliakos. The man helping construct the legal firewall against Greece’s neo-Nazis thus came from a political tradition with deep roots in the country’s junta and its successors. The conditions that allowed Golden Dawn to enter parliament in 2012 did not disappear when its leaders entered prison. Greece has spent years treating neo-Nazism as though it were principally a legal problem. Yet Kasidiaris’s journey exposes the limits of that approach. Parties can disappear while their networks survive. Greece is a country with a remarkable history of resistance to fascism but also an extraordinary capacity for forgetting how deeply Nazism has remained embedded within its political life. Kasidiaris’s return shows that the political environment around Golden Dawn changed sufficiently that many ideas once associated with a neo-Nazi organization no longer sound as politically alien as they did fourteen years ago. Legal barriers may still prevent Kasidiaris himself from appearing on a ballot. However, they cannot dismantle the political and social constituency waiting for him outside the prison gates.

articles.title: What The Flock: Prison Populists and Palantyranny
articles.author: Pine and Roses -- Maine DSA
articles.content: There is a peculiar American humiliation in having to explain why you would like to buy groceries without helping populate a police database. You needed eggs. Apparently, you also owed somebody a record of the trip. Flock Safety’s roadside cameras collect license plates, vehicle characteristics, locations, and timestamps. Pass one and your car can become a searchable observation, available to an investigator with access. The company describes these as snapshots of public vehicle information . Such a modest word, snapshot. A birthday. A beach. Your car passing an intersection while you are trying to get through a Tuesday. A collection of those observations has a different character. It lets an institution ask questions about where you have been. The public road supplies the material. You supply the life. I resent the assumption that either is theirs for the taking. I resent being expected to prove that a trip deserves privacy, as though the default condition of citizenship were a standing invitation to inspect me. And I am tired of the little ceremony in which an industry takes something intimate, calls it data, and waits for the objection to become polite enough to ignore. A road is not a confession. On May 9, 2025, a Texas sheriff’s office searched a month of available records across 83,345 Flock cameras. The reason entered in the log was “had an abortion, search for female.” A woman’s partner had reported her. Investigators collected evidence and asked prosecutors whether they could charge her for taking the medication. They were told they could not. The sheriff and Flock later presented the search as an effort to protect her welfare. But when the woman came to the sheriff’s office a week later, officers questioned her about the abortion and examined her messages. She had come to report a violent assault by the partner who had reported her. He was subsequently charged. The records obtained by the Electronic Frontier Foundation document that sequence. Her need for protection had to get past the state’s interest in her pregnancy. Nobody has to invent a dystopia around this. The investigator typed the reason into a box. The archive was there to be searched. That is what should stick in the throat: how little had to happen before so much became available. The usual reassurances arrive with the weary regularity of an automated email. Your plate is already visible. The records are only kept for a while. The system has rules. Yes, a plate is visible. So is a person sitting in a café. Being seen by another human being does not make your afternoon the rightful property of an investigative system. We used to understand the difference between passing someone on the street and following them home. The distinction does not evaporate because the follower has learned to invoice the city. Flock defaults to thirty days of retention , adjustable by its customers. That is a rolling month of observations, refreshed as people keep driving. Deletion at one end does not stop collection at the other. The archive gets younger. The appetite does not. And rules governing access begin after the first trespass: the decision to make ordinary movement available for inspection. A lock on the filing cabinet cannot supply permission to fill it. An audit can help expose a search that should never have happened; it cannot make the person unsearched. We have been through enough tracking scandals, data-broker revelations, and solemn announcements of revised privacy policies to recognize this transaction. First the intrusion becomes possible. Then it becomes profitable. Eventually, we are invited to a discussion about transparency. By the time the public gets a seat, somebody else is collecting rent on the furniture. Flock has given that familiar entitlement a place beside the road. It is a physical reminder, on the route to work or the way out of town, that somebody has decided your passing should leave a record. You can object at the meeting. Your car can be recorded on the way home. The intimacy of a life often resides in its errands. The pharmacy visited twice. The address you have stopped going to. The place across town where you are trying, quietly, to become someone else. A location does not explain any of these things. It can nevertheless furnish an official with a question you never owed him an answer to. Now consider the protest. In September 2026, 404 Media reported on a Flock webinar that used Denver’s No Kings demonstrations to illustrate event-monitoring tools, including live video. People gathering to contest power became an example of how to equip power to watch them. Even the objection gets a product demo. A demonstration is public because people want to be heard. That does not mean they have volunteered for an institution’s future questions about their associations. A crowd contains the newly persuaded, the unsure, the person attending for the first time, the person whose employer would disapprove. Democracy needs room for people to arrive before they have worked out what arrival might cost. Surveillance sends the bill ahead of time. The prison populist has a solution to this discomfort: imagine that the machinery will always be aimed at somebody worse than you. Give the state more power over them, and it will give you peace. The bargain offers a little borrowed sovereignty, the pleasure of picturing yourself beside the officer rather than inside the search results. Donald Trump put that bargain in the title of his January 2025 order, “Protecting the American People Against Invasion.” The order directed expanded state and local participation in immigration enforcement. The language does its work before any search begins. A population is cast as a threat; restraint becomes something to apologize for. All that remains is to equip the people promising to remove it. The target changes. The equipment stays. This is the prison’s political inheritance: divide people into those entitled to feel safe and those whose submission is supposed to supply the feeling. Then keep expanding the means of submission. A frightened public gets a spectacle of control. The people selling control get a recurring customer. The person who needs housing, treatment, or somewhere to escape a violent partner gets told the budget is complicated. There is an actual corporate bridge between the cage and the cloud. GEO Group operates correctional and detention facilities; its subsidiary BI Incorporated provides electronic monitoring, supervision, and case management under ICE’s Intensive Supervision Appearance Program. GEO reported a renewed award for that work in September 2025 . Confinement and monitoring are two lines of business under one roof. An ankle monitor can be preferable to a cell. That comparison cannot tell us why a person should be monitored at all. When surveillance is imposed on someone who could otherwise remain free, the prison has expanded its reach while congratulating itself on opening the door. Flock offers a more diffuse version of the presumption that people should be made continuously available to authority. No ankle bracelet required. The roadside does the collecting, and a reason to look backward can arrive later. Everyone captured in the archive helps stock the shelf, whether or not an investigator ever takes an interest. There is serious money in stocking it. Flock’s March 2025 funding announcement named Founders Fund among the participants in a $275 million round led by Andreessen Horowitz. Peter Thiel, associated with Founders Fund and a co-founder of Palantir, wrote in 2009 : “I no longer believe that freedom and democracy are compatible.” Whose freedom? The freedom to build the apparatus, certainly. The freedom to refuse it appears to be causing considerably more trouble. Small-government enthusiasm becomes exquisitely selective when the government has a purchase order. The state must keep its filthy hands off the entrepreneur and its eyes on everybody else. Palantir makes software for turning institutional knowledge into action. ICE’s April 2025 award of $30 million for ImmigrationOS specified work on identifying and prioritizing people for apprehension, tracking departures, and managing removals. In January 2026, 404 Media published a user guide for ELITE , another Palantir tool used by ICE, describing maps, dossiers, and confidence scores estimating the reliability of people’s addresses. Confidence scores on where you sleep. An address can be correct and the purpose of finding it abhorrent. AI’s most useful contribution to an authoritarian project may be immaculate obedience: find the person, sort the records, save the official some time. The machine need never develop a taste for cruelty. There is a customer for that. Palantyranny is the rule of the unaccountable over the searchable. It joins the corporation’s power to classify with the state’s power to compel, making a person’s life increasingly visible to authorities whose decisions remain difficult to examine or resist. Your movements become their evidence. Their assumptions become your problem. The machinery may know where you sleep without knowing why you are afraid—and still help decide who comes to your door. Its defining achievement is this unequal exchange: power acquires a detailed account of your life while owing you scarcely an account of itself. Flock and Palantir occupy different parts of this business. What joins the camera to the dossier politically is the claim on your availability: your movements held ready, your circumstances made useful, your life kept within reach. More capable software makes that reach cheaper to exercise. It does nothing to make it deserved. You do not owe Flock a useful Tuesday. You do not owe a sheriff an interesting past. “I have nothing to hide” accepts the wrong obligation. It offers to earn privacy through good behavior. But freedom is not a prize awarded after an inspection, and innocence is no promise that the inspector will leave you alone. The ability to go about your life must survive an official’s curiosity, a contractor’s sales target, and the next election. Nor does the injury wait for an arrest. Sociologist Sarah Brayne’s 2014 research found an association between criminal-justice contact and reduced attachment to record-keeping institutions such as medical care, banks, formal employment, and education. The same pattern did not appear for civic and religious participation. Her account of “system avoidance” identifies a frightening possibility: people can retreat from the institutions they need because those institutions make them visible. Her study concerned criminal-justice contact. The question it leaves beside a roadside camera is what people will give up to avoid the attention they fear. The appointment postponed. The meeting missed. The journey reconsidered until staying home feels like a decision freely made. That last trick is especially foul. Power sets the conditions; you do the shrinking. There may never be an order to disobey or a charge to contest. Just a smaller radius in which to be yourself. So no, the answer is not to design a more considerate dragnet. The answer is to stop collecting ordinary lives against the possibility that somebody powerful will want them later. End the contracts for indiscriminate movement surveillance. Require deletion of the accumulated records and verification that it happened. Close the routes through which another agency or a commercial broker can supply what a community has refused to collect. A particular investigation needs a particular justification. The rest of us are not its raw material. Locally, that means finding the renewal date, demanding the contract, and making the council defend the decision in public. It means asking for removal without allowing the conversation to collapse into a tutorial on settings. A surveillance company is a business. It can lose a customer. We do not have to preserve its revenue stream as a constitutional courtesy. And when the presentation returns to how much the system could know, bring the argument back to what it has no right to know. The errands, the friendships, the private repair work of a human life. The destination that matters desperately to you. The destination that does not matter at all. You went somewhere. None of their business. *** This essay was first published on the author’s Substack, The Armory , on September 10, 2026. It is reprinted here with the author’s permission.
