articles.title: Saudi Arabia’s Yemen Strategy Has Fallen to Pieces
articles.author: Helen Lackner
articles.content: Over the past few weeks, Yemen’s Ansar Allah movement, also known as the Huthis, has launched an offensive and made big territorial gains. The latest turn in the Yemeni civil war could have major implications for the world economy, as it involves one of its most important trade routes through the Red Sea. It certainly poses a big challenge for Yemen’s neighbor Saudi Arabia. Helen Lackner is a leading expert on the politics of Yemen and the author of several books about the country. She spoke to Jacobin about the background to the latest developments and what is likely to happen next. This is an edited transcript from Jacobin’s Long Reads podcast. You can listen to the interview here . Daniel Finn What was the impact of the military campaign against Ansar Allah by the United States and Israel, along with the other steps taken by the Trump administration to impose new sanctions on Yemen? Helen Lackner The US bombing of Yemen was concentrated in the period between March and early May 2025. There was a fifty-two-day bombing campaign targeting the Huthi-ruled areas. Its main impact was to degrade, at least to some extent, the Huthi capacity to launch missiles. But it did not by any means destroy that capacity, as has been demonstrated since then. One important element to talk about in relation to the Trump policy, which has had a much more lasting effect than the bombings, is the designation of Ansar Allah as a “Foreign Terrorist Organization” in March 2025. That kind of move doesn’t have instant results, but it has gradually worsened the living conditions in Huthi-controlled territory and even come close to paralyzing economic activity. Most banks that were previously based in Sanaa, the capital, have now moved their headquarters to the interim capital of Aden. International transactions, which were already very difficult, have become much harder to conduct. That’s relevant first of all in relation to the import of basic goods. Ninety percent of basic staples in Yemen are imported: wheat, rice, tea, etc. The second major impact has been on remittances, which have been the biggest source of income for many Yemenis for a long time. Making the transfer of remittances more difficult is something that affects ordinary Yemenis. The Yemenis living under Huthi control already accounted for two-thirds of the population before the latest offensive. We’re talking about twenty to twenty-five million people. Coming to the Israelis, they launched a number of air strikes in 2025. The most notable one was in August that year, when they managed to kill the prime minister and nine other ministers, plus a number of other senior officials at a meeting. This demonstrated that they now had access to intelligence, something that they previously lacked because Yemen hadn’t been a priority for them. But it also demonstrated that the formal government under the Huthis is not the decision-making entity. The bombing happened last August, more than thirteen months ago now, but the Huthis haven’t yet appointed a new prime minister or any replacements for the ministers and the other officials who were killed. Daniel Finn During the period when Ansar Allah was at war with Israel and the United States, how did that affect the protracted efforts that had been going on to negotiate a formal end to the internal conflict in Yemen, which obviously involves outside actors (notably Saudi Arabia) as well? Helen Lackner There are two elements that need to be looked at. The first is the UN track. We’ve had a UN special envoy since 2011, with the current envoy having been in the role for more than five years now. But the last meeting between the Huthis and the internationally recognized government (IRG) was in 2018, and the UN process has come to a complete standstill. The second element is the direct negotiations between the Saudis and the Huthis that were taking place, to some extent with Omani mediation. If they had been finalized, there would have been an agreement whereby the Huthis would no longer attack Saudi Arabia in any shape or form, while on the other hand, the Huthis would receive compensation for a lot of the war damage between 2015 and 2022 as well as salaries for their staff. The siege on the ports and airports would be lifted, and the Huthis would get a good share of the oil revenues. The deal would not have been a signed and sealed agreement between the Saudis and the Huthis. It would have formally been a deal between the IRG and the Huthis, endorsed by the Saudis. This process was widely believed to have more or less been settled and agreed when the Gaza genocide started. But the Huthis then became involved in supporting the Palestinians and the deal was put on hold. Daniel Finn At the end of last year, there was a short-lived attempt to form a breakaway statelet in southern Yemen. What was the background to that attempt, and why did it unravel so quickly? Was it primarily driven by internal factors or by the Saudi–Emirati rivalry? Helen Lackner It was a bit of both. The anti-Huthi front is officially the IRG, which itself has been badly divided since the war started in 2015. One of the major divisions arises from the southern separatists, who want to return to the situation before 1990, when there were two separate states, the Yemen Arab Republic (in the northwest) and the People’s Democratic Republic of Yemen (in the south and east). The southern separatists themselves come in a multiplicity of forms. But the strongest force among them is a group called the Southern Transitional Council (STC), which the Emiratis had been supporting very heavily since its foundation in 2017. It has been the most active element in undermining the IRG. The Emiratis certainly colluded with, and possibly encouraged, the STC in its bid to take over Hadhramaut and al-Mahra, the far eastern governorates of Yemen. Those governorates had been primarily under the control of the IRG — at least its anti-STC elements — except for the coastal area in Hadhramaut. The STC then mounted a blitzkrieg that in a way resembled what the Huthis have done more recently, and its forces took over the whole of those two governorates within a matter of days in December 2025 The IRG and the Saudis called for them to “withdraw to your previous positions.” Instead they continued their offensive, moving closer and closer to the Saudi border. At that point, the Saudis intervened, bombing a couple of Emirati ships that were bringing in military supplies for the STC in Mukalla, the regional capital, and the port of Hadhramaut. At the same time, the IRG broke its official support agreement with the UAE and demanded that it immediately withdraw its forces, which it did. This was followed by an offensive by the non-STC elements, supported by the Saudis, who pushed back the STC and effectively closed it down throughout the country. The STC itself split into factions. The bigger one joined the IRG and went to Riyadh to prepare for a South–South dialogue that the IRG had announced. They officially dissolved the STC — some say they were forced the make the decision. But another branch of the STC, supported by the Emiratis, continues to exist today. Its leader is believed by everyone to be in the UAE, although he hasn’t made any public appearances. The Emiratis have continued to support this faction in an underhand way. There are also still elements of the STC who remain active and who are objectively now allies with the Huthis, as they have said they won’t fight them. There are widespread reports that they have been selling weapons to the Huthis, and the Huthis have also said that they will not attack them. Basically, you have a situation where this particular group of southern separatists has now split into two. One group is now with the IRG and the other one is more or less underground but claims to be involved in civilian demonstrations and the like. When it comes to Saudi Arabia and the UAE, there has been a tendency to assume that they are great allies, but if you look at history, this is simply not the case. Most of the time they have been rivals. There was a brief moment when they were very close to each other after King Salman came to power in Saudi Arabia with his son, Mohammed bin Salman (MBS), as minister of defense. MBS wanted to become crown prince, and his father also wanted this. He has since achieved this ambition, with a lot of help from the Emiratis. The United States favored his cousin Muhammad bin Nayef, who had long been cooperating with their intelligence agencies, for the role of crown prince. But he was supplanted by MBS, and the UAE’s ambassador to Washington, Yousef Al Otaiba, played a very important role in that outcome. But even back in 2017, there were divisions opening up between Saudi Arabia and the UAE over Yemen. They had started the war in Yemen together in 2015, but by 2017, there were already significant differences between them. Those differences are now apparent in several other countries, including Sudan, Somalia, and Libya, without even mentioning the economic competition between the two states, which is also very important. The situation with the STC and what happened in December last year reflected a combination of internal and external factors, and it would be difficult to determine which aspect was more important than the other. But the Saudi–Emirati divisions will remain an important problem, and Yemen will remain one of the main sites where you can observe the extent of those divisions. Daniel Finn Western politicians and diplomats generally refer to the IRG as if it were the legitimate authority in the country and the Huthis were simply a rebel movement. But what power does that government actually exercise inside Yemen? Helen Lackner This is a very important question that has become all the more important in the light of recent events. The IRG officially controlled about two-thirds of Yemen’s territory before the Huthi advances. But if you look at the map of the country, you will see that much of the area it controlled was desert. The share of the Yemeni population under the IRG’s control was estimated to be about one-third — a maximum of ten million people. Until the war started in 2015, the IRG was simply known as the Yemeni government. Then it was forced out of Sanaa and officially moved to Aden; since then, there have been all kinds of internal conflicts and divisions inside the IRG. It isn’t a cohesive entity. There are different military units, many of which were previously supported by the Emiratis and are under different commanders. For example, the main force on the west coast that has recently been defeated was under the command of Tareq Saleh, the nephew of former President Ali Abdullah Saleh. He has worked with the IRG, but he has never considered himself to be a member of it, although he is a member of the Presidential Leadership Council. The presidency of the IRG is currently an eight-man body with one president and seven vice presidents. The majority of the seven vice presidents are men who control large military units. I hesitate to use the word “warlord,” but it is close to being accurate for some of them. At the civilian level, you have a set of ministers and administrations in the different governorates, but their fundamental problem is finance and the quality of governance. Since November 2022, when the Huthis bombed the ports exporting Yemeni oil on the southern coast, the IRG’s income has more or less disappeared, and it has become almost totally dependent on Saudi financing, international aid, and a very small amount of money raised from taxes. The majority of civil servants have not been paid regularly in any part of Yemen for many years. Although the majority of ministers are actually in Aden, the president has only been there occasionally. He is in Saudi Arabia most of the time. The IRG’s degree of control is minimal and varies from one area to the next. It is more effective in governorates where the local administration has some oil and gas and has been able to keep some of the income and use it to finance services. Even after the collapse of the STC, the IRG remained badly divided. There have been efforts to reorganize the military forces and create some kind of centralized command structure. But what has happened over the last few weeks demonstrated that they were nowhere close to achieving this. The IRG forces disbanded very rapidly and suffered heavy losses. Daniel Finn What impact has the ongoing US war on Iran had on Yemen? To what extent do the Huthis coordinate their actions with Iran and its other allies in the region? Helen Lackner Initially, it had much less impact than anybody expected. Outside observers were expecting the Huthis to take action in support of Iran right from the start, but they did nothing. Although they issued many statements supporting Iran, there was no action. At the end of March, they launched a number of missiles at Israel, but apart from that, they just stated that they could close the Bab al-Mandab Strait if they chose to do so, which would obviously have had a major impact on the world oil market. In a way, this demonstrates that the US bombing campaign of 2025 was probably more effective than many thought at the time, because the Huthis clearly saw it as a priority to discourage Donald Trump from renewing the air strikes. Today, when the Saudis are desperately asking for US support, the Huthis have been talking to US officials, asking them not to start again. Having spent years calling the United States the first and greatest enemy, they have also said that all ships can pass through the Bab el-Mandab except Saudi ones. Another element that’s always worth remembering is the fact that the Huthis are not Iranian proxies. They have their own plans and objectives. Right now, their objective is to strike a blow against Saudi Arabia. Stopping Saudi oil being exported via the Bab al-Mandab and via the East–West pipeline is part of that. It’s convenient for them that this move also supports Iranian efforts to put pressure on the United States by reducing supplies for the world oil market. The Saudis had been exporting about four to five million barrels a day, but that has now been interrupted. Iran and the Huthis are allies; they work together when it suits both sides; but neither is taking orders from the other. There has also been military coordination, even though less military equipment for the Huthis has been arriving, because efforts to stop smuggling on land and by sea have become more effective. The Huthis manufacture most of their equipment themselves, but they do need to import some very sophisticated technical elements. They’re now buying a lot of that material directly on the world market instead of receiving it from Iran. There is plenty of evidence that Iranian and Lebanese military advisers have been helping the Huthis, but they could easily survive without them. They might be slightly less sophisticated, but they could survive without the equipment and the advice. The Huthis have been involved in military activities for more than twenty years now. If they had limited capacities at the beginning, they’ve clearly developed those capacities much further over the years, including some advanced forms of technology. Daniel Finn What was the state of play when the Huthis launched their most recent offensive? Was the offensive something that was widely anticipated in advance? Helen Lackner It was anticipated by some, I would say, but not widely. If you look at what happened in the last three or four months, it seemed to me that the Huthis were likely to launch an offensive within the current period, for several reasons. For one thing, the impact of the terrorist designation had begun having a major effect on daily life in Huthi-controlled areas. The economic situation has greatly worsened and is continuously deteriorating. The World Food Programme, which is the main source of food aid, reduced its contribution dramatically over the last two years, then stopped it altogether last September. This was partly because the Huthis had arrested UN and NGO staff members who were involved in aid distribution but also for political reasons. Of course, the fact that United States Agency for International Development funding completely stopped for Yemen after the early months of 2025 has also had a big impact. You have increased popular dissatisfaction throughout the region, and not just dissatisfaction — people are starving. A second element of concern for the Huthis was what appeared to be a distinct strengthening of the IRG after February this year. As I mentioned, the IRG leaders were reorganizing the military and shifting people between areas. They claimed a few months ago that they had restructured up to 80 percent of their forces and that they were battle-ready. Events clearly proved that this assessment was premature. The third element, of course, is that the Saudis are the main supporters of the IRG after the UAE’s political exit. For the Huthis, the question was, “are the Saudis going to come and make the deal with us, or are they going to go with the IRG and fight us?” The way things were going, with the Iran war and other aspects of the situation, they were concerned that the Saudis would no longer seek to negotiate with them. To attack Saudi Arabia makes a lot of sense from their perspective because there is a baseline of popular support, whereas acting directly in support of Iran is something that has no resonance among Yemenis. Yemenis generally have no sympathy for Iran. The pretext for taking action was the Saudi bombing of the runway at Sanaa airport, when a Huthi delegation was returning on an Iranian flight from Ali Khamenei’s funeral. But this was more of an inconvenience than anything else, since they did not bomb the runway of Hodeidah airport and the delegation was able to land. It was a pretext rather than the main reason. Daniel Finn How significant are the gains that the Huthis have made over the past few weeks? Does it represent a decisive shift in the balance of forces, and what implications might it have for the Saudis? Helen Lackner The big question is whether the gains are reversible or not. If they prove to be irreversible, then they’re very significant. There has been a lot of talk about Huthi control of the Bab al-Mandab. In fact, they already controlled the Red Sea. The big difference now is that if they sit at the bottom of the peninsula, or on Perim Island, they can shoot at anything that comes by with fairly unsophisticated weaponry. Obviously, the fact that they are preventing Saudi ships from going through, exporting oil and bringing back imports, is important. For imports, the Suez Canal is a reasonable substitute. For exports, the Iraqi drone attack on the pipeline last week is more significant, because it is preventing oil from reaching Yanbu, the Saudi port on the Red Sea coast. The Saudis can still export up to two million barrels a day. But by going through the Bab al-Mandab, they had been exporting between four and five million barrels a day over the last few months. Going through the Suez Canal is much less convenient because the large oil carriers, known as VLCCs, cannot go through the canal fully loaded. The oil has to be taken to the bottom of the canal and either transferred to smaller ships or through a small pipeline and then reloaded when it reaches the Mediterranean Sea. Eighty percent of Saudi exports go to East Asia, so after arriving in the Mediterranean, they have to go all the way past Gibraltar, around Africa, and back up to Asia. This route is much less convenient and much more expensive. The balance of forces between the Huthis and the anti-Huthi elements will depend on what happens next and whether the latter can reorganize themselves and receive the air support and other forms of support they need from the Saudis or other players. But air strikes do not win wars without land forces, so unless the Yemeni land forces are reorganized so they can be more effective, there will not be any reversal. I wouldn’t like to say that the change in the balance of forces will prove decisive in the long term. My perception when this fighting started in August was that we were back more or less where we were in 2015, at the beginning of a long and nasty war. At the moment, unfortunately, I see no reason to change my mind on that, although I hope that I’m wrong. Daniel Finn What are the social and humanitarian conditions facing the people of Yemen after the latest turn of the war, and how are they likely to develop in the coming months? Helen Lackner It’s very important to remember that the humanitarian situation is disastrous, regardless of what happens for the country’s leaders. Yemen was the world’s worst humanitarian crisis for a number of years. It lost that title, not because anything improved in Yemen but because things got so much worse in Sudan and other places. Starvation is becoming a major issue throughout the country. As I mentioned earlier, the situation is even worse in the Huthi-controlled area, for two-thirds or more of the population, than it is in the IRG area. But in both areas, it is very bad. The UN’s humanitarian aid appeal for this year, which is smaller than last year’s, has only been financed at 23 percent by the end of September. This is very low, even compared to last year, which was already very bad. People were suffering enormously even before the latest turn of events. Now, with the developments in the southwest of the country and the military activity, about 150,000 people have been displaced at the latest count, on top of the four to five million people displaced over the last ten years. Given the shortage of aid, it’s even more difficult for them to find places to stay, whether temporarily or permanently. So many people have been interviewed saying that they’ve just run with the clothes on their backs and bullets flying overhead, and the number of displaced people is likely to increase. Those who are still in their villages but have been caught up in the fighting are going to try and escape if they possibly can, so long as you have these active military fronts.

articles.title: Greed and Economic Desperation Are Fueling Sudan’s Civil War
articles.author: Ahmed Ismat Ahmed
articles.content: I used to pass the biscuit factory in Soba without going in. People I knew went in for a twelve-hour shift on a line that smelled of sugar and oil. In 2021, the number that stuck was 1,500 pounds for the shift. In Haj Yousif, where Iqbal lived, the rent for a single room was 30,000 pounds a month. You had to work twenty factory days just to cover rent. Meanwhile, the Rapid Support Forces were offering people 15,000 a day, a uniform, and a phone. Those three numbers explain more about Sudan’s war than any map I have been shown since. What happened in Sudan was not primarily a story of people choosing violence. It was a story of people choosing the wage that was available. A Bus That Does Not Come Iqbal sold tea in front of the medical campus at the University of Khartoum, setting up with three low stools, a few plastic chairs that did not match, a kettle that was black at the bottom, and a sugar jar with a spoon that was always wet. She kept her coins in a small tin. She lived in Haj Yousif. Traveling to the university from her home involved hours on buses, not to mention the time spent walking and standing in the heat for a bus that does not come. She did it every day. Her husband had run away — her choice of words — to fight with Abdelaziz al-Hilu in South Kordofan. I do not know the full story of what took him. What I know is that the farm outside the city had stopped paying for a life inside it, and that a rifle and a cause offer the kind of wage a collapsing farm cannot. Iqbal stayed with their four children, who would be fed or not fed depending on how the day went. Around her, on the same stretch of pavement, Asyaa ran two kettles at once, while Fatouma sold tea and roasted nuts and knew which patients in Shar al-Hawadith had not eaten. The women had come in numbers when the farms stopped paying. Men left for the mines or the militias. Khartoum needed cheap food, cheap warmth, and cheap care for students who could not afford a meal or companions waiting a week in a hospital corridor. The city got what it needed, but the women who provided it were deemed illegal. The local authority sent a pickup with two or three men in uniforms that never looked fully clean. They seized the chairs, the kettle, the sugar, sometimes the gas cylinder, too. You had to go to their office and pay to get your own things back. We called the practice kasha . The state had decided that Iqbal’s labor was not a business. It was an obstruction — and what it could not ignore, it taxed. When we saw the truck turn the corner, we hid her stools behind the labs. A different truck offered her neighbor 15,000 pounds a day and a story he could tell his family. Two days of that wage was a month of rent on her street. You did not need a lecture on identity to explain why a boy answered the recruitment call. In a city where the state had made survival illegal and a collapsing currency had made the factory irrelevant, a soldier’s wage was the only thing that replaced the state. In 2018, a man sat at her stall like any customer. He noticed her phone, which was basic and worn at the edges. Over the course of several visits, the talk moved toward money, and he offered her a new phone and weekly payments of real money. He wanted her to sit among us and report what the students said: who was organizing, who came and went. She refused the offer. She did not tell us at the time and carried that refusal alone until the regime fell. When she finally mentioned it, I asked why she had never said. She said she did not want us to worry or do something stupid. Mostly — and this is the sentence that has not left me — she did not want fear to change what we were doing at the gate. There was a small room in the pharmacy faculty where leftover donated drugs went to patients from the hospital next door. The tea women brought their children. A registrar looked at a sick child on a stool, and a pharmacist walked out with the medicine. There were no forms, and nobody paid 15,000 a day for any of it. Guns and Gold I sat with a miner from Jebel Amer whose hands were burned from mercury during the sit-in in May 2019, in the place we called Kolombia, the open ground behind the railway tracks. He said the RSF took 30 percent of everything. The mine had closed after fighting with Musa Hilal’s men, and he had come to Khartoum with nothing. He joined the sit-in. He said if the RSF came, he would fight. On June 3, he disappeared, and I never found him afterward. After clashes with Hilal, the RSF took Jebel Amer. At the peak, they were extracting something like forty kilograms a day. The metal was processed with mercury, then flown from Khartoum airport to Dubai — sometimes a hundred kilograms a flight, once a week — with no customs paperwork on the Sudanese side. From Dubai, it entered the global gold market, occasionally passing through European refineries that did not ask where it came from. Investigators later put the annual take at more than a billion US dollars. From 2015, the same force was sending men to Yemen for Saudi and Emirati pay. The UAE had been cultivating Sudanese military figures since the early 2010s; when the Yemen war needed ground forces composed of men who could move fast and not ask questions, they called the RSF leader Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo, better known as Hemedti. Estimates of the deployment range from 14,000 to 40,000 fighters between 2015 and 2020. The pay was in dollars, which meant you could recruit faster than the army, buy equipment, and build a buffer against any future rupture with Khartoum. Fighters rotated home having been trained in urban combat and logistics. I remember the new trucks in Khartoum that year. I did not know the money was Gulf money, although I knew the men who had burned villages in Darfur were moving through my city as if they owned it. The RSF was not, by this point, a paramilitary force sustained by weapons. It was a mining and logistics operation that maintained an army. The weapons were evidence of its power, which derived from gold. With that gold, Hemedti built an empire that ran parallel to the state instead of through it. Al Junaid, the family conglomerate, became one of the largest mining and construction operations in the country. In October 2019, people in Talodi, South Kordofan, set fire to one of its cyanide plants after the runoff poisoned their water and killed their cattle. Guards opened fire, but the crowd burned it anyway. Investigators at Global Witness later traced RSF payments moving through UAE-based front companies into accounts at the National Bank of Abu Dhabi and documented the purchase of more than 900 Toyota Hilux and Land Cruiser vehicles. There were real estate holdings across the capital, farms in Darfur, and a trucking fleet. The gold bought more than guns — it bought a parallel economy, booked in Dubai. Russia’s Wagner Group arrived around 2017 for the same metal, exchanging military training and equipment for mining concessions in RSF territory. When the US Treasury sanctioned those operations in 2020, the networks reorganized through UAE-based intermediaries. The buyer did not change. Swissaid, reading the UAE’s own trade figures for 2024, found that Dubai imported twenty-nine metric tons of gold from Sudan that year, a big increase from seventeen metric tons the year before. According to the same figures, eighteen additional metric tons came from Chad and nine from Libya, two countries that are not famous for their gold mines but serve as transit routes for metal moved out of RSF territory. Supply and Demand In September this year, Michael Waltz and Massad Boulos argued in Foreign Policy that peace in Sudan can only come after a weapons embargo, extending the old Darfur ban of 2005 across the whole country. Drones, they write, do not stop at Darfur’s border, and they are right about the geography. On September 11, the United Nations Security Council extended existing measures for one month, until October 9. Washington has been pushing for a nationwide ban, while Moscow opposes any expansion. Waltz and Boulos frame the problem as one of supply: more than a dozen countries are feeding both sides, and an extension of the ban will block them from doing so. Some of that is right. But an arms embargo addresses a supply problem — the flow of weapons — while the political economy of militia recruitment is a problem of demand. The UAE is not just one supplier among others. It is the buyer of last resort for Sudanese gold and the logistics node for the air bridge into Darfur. Dubai’s refineries process the metal, and the same financial infrastructure enables the flights.The profit is not incidental to the war. A force paid from the mine, through Dubai, does better when the country is in pieces. None of this is a defense of the Sudanese army. It has a history of coups, of alliances with Islamists, of violence in the peripheries. But a ruined army still has to pretend it employs people on behalf of a state. It still needs ports, a capital, a population that eats if the flag is going to mean anything. There are steps that could be taken in response. One important move would be to complement the weapons ban with Kimberley-style certification for Sudanese gold at the point when it enters refineries. Another would be to apply sanctions on UAE-based entities that form part of the air bridge and on the front companies and bank accounts that convert the metal into Toyotas. Filling the Silence Iqbal had to leave Haj Yousif when the fighting reached her neighborhood. She went to her sister’s place in Omdurman, not to work but to wait. I called her from Halfa, near the Egyptian border, after I left. The line is always bad, always dropping in the middle of a sentence so you do not know if she heard you. At first, I talked too much, filling the silence the way you do when you are afraid the other person has gone. Then I learned to wait. I kept asking whether she had found a stall. She had not. She said the city was not hers. Her voice came through tired but still the same. I can still do the arithmetic from Soba to Haj Yousif in my head: 1,500 for twelve hours; 30,000 for a room; 15,000 for a day with a gun . The truck paid better. She asked if I was eating anyway.

articles.title: Xi on his DC visit: ‘China and the US should be partners not rivals’
articles.author: Abdul Rahman
articles.content: China’s President Xi Jinping concluded his three-day state visit to the US on Friday, September 25, with hopes of enhanced cooperation and partnership between the world’s two largest economies. Xi arrived in the US on Wednesday and received a large-scale welcome from President Donald Trump. Though this was their third in-person meeting it was Xi’s first state visit to the US in over a decade. On Thursday, the leaders had a long in-person conversation in the White House and finished the day with a state dinner with 130 guests, including tech executives. Though the US is yet to release its version of the official proceedings, reports indicate they discussed a range of outstanding issues such as the dispute over trade and tariffs, cooperation in Artificial Intelligence, the issue of Taiwan, and the US-Israeli war on Iran. During the meeting with Trump, Xi called for strategic stability in the China-US relationship which will benefit both countries and the people around the world, Xinhua reported. “China and the US should be partners, not rivals,” Xi said. Xi’s statement comes at a time when the two countries are negotiating a longer trade deal after briefly facing each other in a tariff war last year. Both countries agreed to extend their temporary trade truce which halted the tariff war till January to give their negotiators more time. The so-called Busan Trade Truce was set to expire in November this year. Xi hoped that “both sides would stay committed to the principles of mutual benefit and win-win cooperation and promote the sustained, stable and sound development of China-US economic and trade relations.” Technology and AI Successive administrations in the US have characterized China’s advancements in technology and other economic sectors as a threat to American interests and have tried to curb them by restricting its access to technology. In his attempt to address such apprehensions, Xi proposed that “both sides work towards a relationship featuring cooperation as the mainstay, moderate competition, manageable differences, and the promise of peace.” Talking about the competition in the development of Artificial Intelligence (AI), Xi offered increased coordination and cooperation between the countries as a way of mutual benefit. While emphasizing that “two sides should maintain human control over AI technologies, uphold people-centered approach and the principle of using AI for good” he proposed greater exchange of information to “prevent any misuse and abuse of AI.” Read more: The AI frontier asks to be paced: anatomy of a panic Xi also expressed hope that Chinese companies “are treated fairly in the US” while inviting more US companies to invest in China. “Working together, we can lengthen the list of cooperation and shorten the list of issues” he underlined. The US has sanctioned or put a large number of Chinese companies, including its AI firms on various watch lists in recent years, after accusing them of working with the Chinese armed forces or being involved in the so-called technology theft . Notably, however, major US tech and finance executives such as Jensen Huang of Nvidia, Mark Zuckerberg of Meta, Eric Yuan of Zoom, Kelly Ortberg of Boeing, Larry Fink of Blackrock, Sam Altman of OpenAI, Satya Nadella of Microsoft, Sundar Pichai of Google, Jeff Bezos of Amazon, and Elon Musk of SpaceX and Tesla, were present at the state dinner for Xi’s visit hosted at the White House on Thursday, September 24, though no details of cooperation between US and Chinese tech firms have emerged. Taiwan Reiterating China’s resolve to “safeguard national reunification and territorial integrity,” Xi expressed hope that the US will “adhere to the correct position on opposing ‘Taiwan independence’ and handle the Taiwan question with caution.” China has repeatedly accused the US of promoting the separatist cause in Taiwan, despite officially adhering to “one China policy.” The US under Trump has sold or agreed to sell billions of dollars’ worth of weapons to Taiwan in complete disregard of China’s objections. China has also accused the US and its allies in the region of promoting an arms race by deploying advanced weapon systems close to its borders. Xi said if the US follows the correct position on Taiwan it “will enable both the countries to lay a solid foundation for their strategic cooperation and the development of their bilateral relationship.” US-Israeli war on Iran China has refused to intervene or get involved in the US-Israeli war on Iran, despite Trump’s repeated calls for them to do so. China has maintained the war was unnecessary and repeatedly warned against its prolongation. It has supported the interim peace deal signed in June under international mediation. Xi reiterated this position during his visit to the US, expressing hope that both Iran and the US would soon return to the Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) and end the war. Xi claimed that “China-US cooperation may not solve every problem in the world, but without it, it would be hard to solve many of the world’s problems” and proposed more dialogue and “mechanisms of crisis communication and prevention” between their armed forces. Read more: No new talks with the US until the previous conditions are met, says Iran Trump said his meeting with Xi on Thursday was “great” also claiming they have maintained close communication. Trump also agreed that “continued dialogue” with China is necessary to reach agreement on significant issues.

articles.title: ‘Cuba is not a threat, the blockade is’: Díaz-Canel replies to Trump
articles.author: Pablo Meriguet
articles.content: In his address to the UN General Assembly, US President Donald Trump said that the Cuban government is a failed state currently under enormous pressure: “My administration seeks a fundamental change in the situation in Cuba… It is an absolute failed state… and it will fall. Marco Rubio is leading the negotiations.” In response, the Cuban delegation stood up and walked out of the plenary session in protest. Trump continued : “Cuba is a haven for foreign adversaries who threaten America right on our doorstep… The Cuban regime has also spent decades coordinating with left-wing radicals and communist networks here in the United States… They have cultivated ties with subversive and radical groups.” The remarks did not go over well in Havana, where the government has categorically rejected the US right-wing leader’s statements. Leading the response is the country’s president, Miguel Díaz-Canel, who asserted that freedom in Cuba is non-negotiable. “Freedom came to Cuba on January 1, 1959, [the date the Cuban Revolution began], and we are not going to lose it; we are going to defend it. Once again, we are seeing the true face of that empire and its contempt for the peoples of Latin America – and in particular for Cuba and the Cuban Revolution – because of what it represents.” Díaz-Canel made the remarks on a program called Criterio Compartido on Radio Rebelde . In them, Díaz-Canel described Trump’s statements as “arrogant,” “high-handed,” and “interventionist.” He also asserted that behind Trump’s thinking lies a justification for a certain view of US imperialism: “what most underpins that genocidal, criminal, and contemptuous mindset toward Cuba and the Cuban people.” Regarding the label of “failed state,” the leader of the Communist Party of Cuba said : “They are always trying to label us a failed state to shift the blame for the genocide they are committing with that intensified and prolonged blockade.” Díaz-Canel is referring not only to the long and sustained economic and commercial blockade that the United States unilaterally imposed on Cuba in an effort to defeat the revolution that began in 1959. In US President Donald Trump’s first term, he imposed an additional 243 sanctions on the Caribbean island and added Cuba to the State Sponsors of Terrorism (SSoT) list, which devastated the Cuban economy. In January 2026, Trump further tightened the grip by imposing an energy blockade on Cuba. Since early 2026, following the US attack on Venezuela that resulted in the capture of President Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, and the deaths of more than 100 people – including several dozen Cubans – Cuba lost one of its main energy partners, which used to supply crude oil to the Cuban power grid. Since then, only one Russian ship has managed to circumvent the US blockade; the United States is currently threatening to impose additional tariffs on any country that sells fuel to Cuba. This has triggered Cuba’s worst energy crisis, which is hindering the normal operation of hospitals, schools, and food production, among other essential activities. Cuba has denounced the blockade as a form of “silent genocide,” specifically because of the direct humanitarian consequences it is having on the civilian population, which has seen a reduction not only in its electricity supply but also in access to surgeries, water, food, and so on. In this regard, Díaz-Canel has once again emphasized on X that Cuba does not pose a threat to the United States; rather, it is the United States that is endangering Cuba’s civilian population: “Unable to justify the punishment against the people of Cuba and its genocidal economic war, the US president repeats at the UN that Cuba poses a threat. Lies are the weapon of those who refuse to accept the Cuban people’s right to self-determination.” He concluded : “We will continue to fight for peace, defend our sovereignty, and work together to overcome the ruthless aggression imposed on us by the US government. Cuba is not a threat, the blockade is.”

articles.title: German students say ‘we don’t want to go to war’
articles.author: Ana Vračar
articles.content: Thousands of students across Germany were once again on strike against conscription and militarization on Friday, September 25. Actions took place in at least 100 localities as young people demanded a sharp turn from the government’s chosen path. “We don’t want to be forced into military service and we don’t want to go to war,” the students wrote in declaration after their last strike in May. Read more: German students expand their strike against conscription and militarization to 150 cities This is the fourth time students have exchanged classrooms for streets since the end of 2025 . The mobilization has strengthened in resistance to the Merz administration’s plans to build the “strongest conventional army in Europe” – including by drawing more people into the Bundeswehr, the German armed forces. While authorities insist military recruitment remains voluntary, students have warned of a clear tendency toward outright conscription. Local strike committees and activists also emphasized the widespread repression ahead of actions. This included scheduling of exams on strike days and locking-in students on school grounds, they pointed out. Billions for the Bundeswehr , cuts for schools and youth services Over recent months, the government has sent thousands of questionnaires to map voluntary interest in joining the armed forces. According to German media, the response has been underwhelming: tens of thousands of students have disclaimed no interest whatsoever. Not even a multi-million-euro budget allocated to promoting the army has been able to shake this opinion. “They sell us war service as an ‘adventure’ while we know that what awaits us is coertion, humiliation, sexism, right-wing extremism, and racism,” the student declaration adds. Instead of taking the message seriously, authorities recently advanced the implementation of medical checks among their targeted population, drawing further frustration from students. “We don’t want compulsory questionnaires, fines, draft physical examinations, conscription assessment centres across the country, nor planned integration of the Federal Volunteer Service into military service,” they wrote. “These are means to prepare the reintroduction of the draft and thus another war originating from Germany.” “In case of conscription, we’ll be trained as cannon fodder, forced into the trenches,” students added. “War costs us our lives, while corporations like Rheinmetall make record profits.” Read more: Ulrike Eifler: ‘The workplace is a place where we have to fight against war’ Students on strike have expressed solidarity with other ongoing struggles against militarization and budget cuts. They stated they would join peace demonstrations planned for early October in Berlin and Stuttgart, as well as a trade union-backed mobilization against budget cuts on Saturday, September 26. Their decision reflects the widespread understanding that youth and education services are among those impacted by this round of austerity. According to junge Welt , the federal ministry responsible for education will face close to €1 billion in cuts – while €140 billion will be made available for so-called defense in 2027. “Every tank, every rocket we pay for with dilapidated schools and social cuts,” students remarked.

articles.title: Trump’s war on the ICC is bigger than Netanyahu, with Noura Erakat
articles.author: Zoe Alexandra
articles.content: The Trump administration’s assault on the ICC isn’t just about protecting Netanyahu from war crimes prosecution. It’s about preserving “imperial impunity” – Israel’s just “the smokescreen,” says Noura Erakat, professor of criminal justice and Africana studies at Rutgers University and human rights attorney. She traces Washington’s bipartisan refusal to ratify the Rome Statute to explain why the International Criminal Court has spent two decades indicting mostly African and Arab leaders. The 2024 warrants for Netanyahu and former Israeli defense minister Yoav Gallant just show the court “between a rock and a hard place”: finally give up its legitimacy entirely, or face destruction by the US. Now more than a dozen ICC judges, prosecutors, and the court’s president have been sanctioned, as Washington reportedly prepares sanctions against the entire institution, with Secretary of State Marco Rubio calling it an “intolerable threat” to US sovereignty. Can the court survive a war with Washington? Should it? And why do Global South states stay invested in a court that’s clearly stacked against them? Plus: Erakat describes her arrest at a Palm Beach County budget hearing on their $1 billion-plus investment in Israel bonds; warns that Gaza’s Board of Peace could become a blueprint to replace the UN; and explains why she believes, even as public opinion on Palestine shifts, “there’s no way to be safe in this moment by hiding.” Watch full episodes of BT Live, join breakthroughnews.org as a member today!

articles.title: Bernie Sanders and US Democrats Accuse Trump of Trying to Interfere in Brazil’s Elections
articles.content: Imagem do presidente Donald Trump projetada no ato bolsonarista no dia 7 de setembro, na Avenida Paulista, em São Paulo. | Crédito: Miguel Schincariol / AFP Senator Bernie Sanders and 30 Democratic members of the U.S. House of Representatives sent a letter to Secretary of State Marco Rubio accusing the Donald Trump administration of waging a pressure campaign against Brazil ahead of the first round of vote on October 4. The letter was sent Thursday, September 24. Illinois Congresswoman Delia C. Ramirez led the congressional effort. In it, the lawmakers say that recent actions from the White House “point toward an apparent effort to interfere with, and potentially undermine, Brazil’s general election in October.” They demand that Washington commit to recognizing the certified election results. In particular, the letter cited the Oval Office meeting between Trump and Senator and presidential candidate Flávio Bolsonaro in May. According to the letter, the son of former President Jair Bolsonaro used the occasion to ask the United States to designate the Brazilian drug gangs, Primeiro Comando da Capital and the Comando Vermelho, as foreign terrorist organizations. The White House followed through with the request shortly thereafter. The lawmakers said that Brazilian authorities fear this measure could be used to justify sanctions and other extraterritorial actions. The group also noted that Trump’s military strikes in Latin America were justified, in particular, by alleged threats from such organizations. “We are writing to express our grave concern regarding the Administration’s coordinated effort to threaten our strategic alliance with Brazil and undermine the Western Hemisphere’s second-largest democracy ahead of its upcoming presidential election in October 2026,” reads an excerpt from the document. The letter also points out that, “Rather than helping defend Brazilian democracy, the United States is acting as an agent of interference and destabilization—using diplomatic, economic, and political pressure in ways that risk weakening the country’s democratic institutions, undermining confidence in Brazil’s electoral process, and inflicting further damage on our relationship with a strategic U.S. ally and trading partner.” According to the document, this pattern of conduct not only risks the integrity of electoral processes in individual countries, “but also progressively eroding electorates’ confidence in democratic processes and institutions across the region.” The lawmakers also note that the “sustained, multifaceted campaign of interference and destabilization in Brazil” is driven by the steep tariff hikes promoted by Trump and by U.S. sanctions against Supreme Federal Court justices. The White House’s actions are characterized as an “extraordinary infringement” of Brazilian sovereignty. Interference by the Trump administration in the Brazilian election has been speculated about for months. It has now intensified to the point where the Brazilian Intelligence Agency had to produce a confidential report, disclosed by the newspaper Folha de S. Paulo, raising the possibility of foreign influence in the electoral process to a “critical level.” The reelection campaign of President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva has petitioned the Brazilian Supreme Court and the Supreme Electoral Court over the matter. Translated by Panamerican Dispatch.

articles.title: What is the UN actually good for? with Vijay Prashad
articles.author: Zoe Alexandra
articles.content: Can the United Nations be saved? Should it be? As world leaders and war criminals gather for the 81st session of the UN General Assembly in New York, Vijay Prashad, executive director of the Tricontinental Institute for Social Research, says that despite today’s gangster rule by the likes of Donald Trump and Benjamin Netanyahu, the UN Charter still sets the standard for judging powerful states, making it “the most important treaty document that the world has ever had” – even with the institution built on it in shambles. Prashad slams Secretary-General António Guterres’s failure to get “creative” to end the genocide in Gaza or to stand up to Trump on Iran, instead opening a free lane for the US president who has “put a loaded gun on the table and has threatened the world.” After the US denied visas to the Palestinians for a second year and heavily restricted Iran’s delegation, Prashad makes the case for moving the high-level UNGA out of the US: “New York doesn’t deserve it anymore,” he says, offering alternatives in Geneva or Nairobi. “Let’s move it to the Global South. articles.title: Trump needs China, Xi is playing the long game, with Amanda Yee
articles.author: Rania Khalek
articles.content: Chinese President Xi Jinping “holds all the cards” as he meets with Trump on Thursday, says Amanda Yee, host of BreakThrough News’ The China Report. She joins Zoe Alexandra and Rania Khalek to break down Xi’s first White House visit in 11 years. With Trump facing a massively unpopular war on Iran, surging inflation, growing resistance to ICE terror – and with US midterms weeks away – Washington wants quick deals it can sell as big wins. But Yee says Beijing is playing a longer game, with massive implications for the global future. Take AI: Washington’s Pax Silica forces allies to pick sides, while Beijing’s open model is available to all and centered on the Global South. Two systems, representing “the choice that’s in front of the world right now.” Despite a stated pivot away from China as a military priority, Yee points to Latin America and Iran as proxy fronts where the Trump administration continues to target Beijing. Meanwhile the military encirclement of China continues, from US bases in South Korea, Okinawa and the Philippines, to Japan’s remilitarization and expanding war games like RIMPAC and Freedom Shield. But Yee says “the Cold War on China is a bipartisan affair.” From TikTok to Huawei to BYD, she traces the pattern of trumping up national security threats to mask efforts to protect US companies from competition. It’s all part of the same Red Scare targeting BT News, subpoenaed by the House Ways and Means Committee in an effort to paint anti-war voices as Chinese assets. articles.title: Pakistan’s Imran Khan crackdown: hospitals brace for ‘mass casualties’
articles.author: Rania Khalek
articles.content: Why is Pakistan’s military so afraid of Imran Khan? With Islamabad on lockdown and 35,000 additional troops deployed to stop the September 27 march in support of the imprisoned ex-prime minister. Junaid S. Ahmad, professor of religion and world politics and director of the Center for Study of Islam and Decoloniality, tells Rania Khalek and Zoe Alexandra the 2022 US-backed regime-change operation meant to neutralize the country’s most popular politician instead gave rise to a movement bigger than Khan himself: a new opposition coalition, TTAP, including the left-wing Awami Workers Party, as Khan’s PTI party has shattered the army’s legitimacy in Punjab. Ahmad says Pakistan, under military rule in all but name, has become “nothing less than a police state.” Its only legitimacy, he says, comes from Washington and Rawalpindi, the home of the army’s headquarters. And with past demonstrations ending in massacres and the Shehbaz Sharif-Asim Munir regime telling hospitals to prepare for a “mass-casualty event,” Ahmad explains why this Sunday’s march has gone global, with solidarity protests planned from Washington to London to Kuala Lumpur, and why Khan refuses to call it off, even as his sisters and wife are jailed.
